title: Monochromatic vs Dark Mode
lede: One restricts hue, the other restricts value. They are different constraints and they fail in opposite directions.
verdict: Monochromatic uses a single hue and varies only its lightness — every grey on the page is the same blue. Dark mode uses neutral surfaces and varies value in tight steps, reserving colour for one accent.
brief: Monochromatic is a palette rule: take one hue, derive nine values from near-white to near-black, and build everything from that ramp. The page reads as tinted rather than coloured, and hierarchy comes from how far up the ramp an element sits.

Dark mode is a contrast rule: surfaces step from #0e1116 to #1d232c, borders sit at 8 percent white, and a single accent is reserved for anything interactive. Nothing is tinted; the neutral is the point, because a dark interface has to stay out of the way of content and images.

dimensions.b: One accent, used only on controls

whenA: The brand already has one strong colour and you want the interface to inherit it
The page is a document or a report where status colours are not needed
You want a distinctive look from a very small token set — nine values, no colour decisions
whenB: The product is used at night or alongside media, where a bright page is hostile
You need status colours and cannot afford to lose them
The interface is data-heavy and the content should dominate the chrome
promptDelta: For monochromatic, give the model the hue and the number of steps and tell it that no other hue may appear — including in borders and shadows, which are where a stray blue usually sneaks in. For dark mode, give the surface steps as exact hex values and state that the accent is for interactive elements only; without that clause a model will tint headings and borders and the page stops reading as neutral.
